articles.headline: OFAC Updates Iran Sanctions List, Reinforcing Economic Pressure
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced an update to its Iran sanctions list on November 9, 2026. This action is part of the ongoing U.S. strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran.

While specific details of the updated designations were not immediately released, such actions typically involve adding individuals or entities to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List, or other sanctions lists. These designations aim to disrupt financial networks and activities deemed to support Iran's destabilizing behavior.

The U.S. Treasury Department consistently uses its sanctions authorities to target those involved in Iran's nuclear program, ballistic missile development, support for terrorism, and human rights abuses.

articles.headline: U.S. Imposes New Iran-Related Designations Amidst Regional Tensions
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action targets individuals and entities involved in activities that support the Iranian regime.

These designations are part of a broader effort to counter Iran's illicit financial activities and its support for regional proxy groups. The U.S. has consistently applied sanctions to limit Iran's access to the international financial system.
The move comes as regional tensions remain high, with the U.S. reiterating its commitment to preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon and curbing its malign influence.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organizations; Imposes New Cuba Sanctions
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of designations on November 5, 2026, targeting cyber-related threats and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new sanctions against Cuba. This action underscores the U.S. commitment to combating illicit activities across multiple fronts.

The Cuba designations are accompanied by the publication of a Cuba-related determination, further tightening restrictions on the island nation. These measures are part of the Trump administration's escalated economic campaign against Cuba, aiming to force political change and address what it views as human rights abuses and support for Venezuela.

The cyber-related designations aim to disrupt malicious cyber activities that pose a threat to U.S. national security and financial systems, while the transnational criminal organization designations target groups involved in various illicit enterprises.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran Sanctions, Amends Venezuela General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to existing Iran-related listings. This action is part of ongoing efforts to pressure the Iranian regime.

In addition to the Iran-focused measures, OFAC also issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. This amendment likely provides clarification or adjustments to authorized activities involving Venezuela, reflecting the dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy.

An Iran-related OFAC Alert was also published, signaling potential new risks or compliance considerations for businesses and individuals engaging with Iran. These alerts are crucial for ensuring adherence to evolving sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License, Adjusting Permitted Activities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026. This amendment modifies previously authorized transactions and activities involving Iran.

General Licenses are crucial tools in sanctions programs, allowing for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited. Amendments can either broaden or narrow the scope of permitted activities, often in response to evolving policy considerations or humanitarian concerns.
Businesses and individuals engaged in Iran-related activities are advised to review the amended General License carefully to ensure ongoing compliance with U.S. sanctions regulations.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting entities in North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to counter illicit activities and human rights abuses in both regions.

The North Korea designations are part of ongoing efforts to curb the regime's weapons of mass destruction programs and its illicit revenue generation activities. The U.S. continues to pressure Pyongyang through sanctions to denuclearize.

The DRC-related designations likely address concerns related to corruption, human rights violations, or the exploitation of natural resources in the country. Such designations underscore the U.S. commitment to promoting stability and good governance globally.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. These updates provide crucial guidance for financial institutions and other entities subject to U.S. sanctions regulations.

The FAQs clarify compliance obligations related to handling transactions involving sanctioned parties or jurisdictions, and the proper procedures for reporting such activities to OFAC. Accurate and timely reporting is a cornerstone of effective sanctions enforcement.
These amendments are vital for ensuring that financial institutions and businesses remain compliant with OFAC's complex regulatory framework, minimizing the risk of penalties for violations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New General Licenses for Iran and Russia, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026, while also issuing new general licenses for Iran and Russia. Concurrently, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

The issuance of new general licenses for Iran and Russia suggests specific carve-outs or authorizations for certain types of transactions, potentially related to humanitarian aid or other limited engagements. These licenses are critical for navigating complex sanctions landscapes.

The removal of designations for Belarus and North Korea indicates a reassessment of specific entities or individuals, potentially due to changes in their activities or broader policy shifts. OFAC also issued amended FAQs to provide further clarity on these changes.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA)
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 19, 2026, under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). This marks a significant step in the U.S. government's efforts to combat intellectual property theft that poses a threat to national security and economic health.

Three entities were added to OFAC's Non-SDN Menu-Based Sanctions List: BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE I VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP, BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN PHASE II VENTURE CAPITAL CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP, and BEIJING QIJI CHUANGTAN ZHIYUAN ENTERPRISE MANAGEMENT CENTER LIMITED PARTNERSHIP. These entities are linked to Beijing Qiji Chuangtan Beijing Investment Management Co Ltd.

OFAC also issued PAIPA General License 1, authorizing transactions pursuant to cyber-related sanctions regulations, and PAIPA General License 2, authorizing the wind-down of transactions involving certain entities blocked on October 19, 2026. These designations block all property and interests in property of the sanctioned parties within U.S. jurisdiction and generally prohibit U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with them.

articles.headline: U.S. Inflation Rises Faster Than Expected, Rattling Wall Street and Boosting Rate Hike Expectations
body: U.S. inflation rose faster than anticipated in October, with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) increasing by 0.4% on a monthly basis, exceeding economists' forecasts of 0.3%. This surge was primarily driven by rising food and energy prices, which climbed 0.5% and 0.7% respectively.

The discouraging inflation report immediately impacted Wall Street, with U.S. stocks stumbling in early trading. The S&P 500 fell 0.2%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 0.4%, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.1% lower. Bond yields also jumped, with the 10-year Treasury yield rising to 4.98% from 4.88%, as traders increased their forecasts for future interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

Federal Reserve policymaker Christopher Waller indicated that a stronger policy move, potentially a half-point hike in U.S. interest rates, might be necessary if core CPI inflation remains around 0.3% or higher. Markets are now fully pricing in a December interest rate increase. Meanwhile, the UK also saw business growth reach an eight-month high, though cost pressures remained elevated due to energy, transport, and raw material costs.

articles.headline: Iraq Bars Iranian Football Team's Plane from Landing in Basra Due to US Sanctions
body: Iraq's Civil Aviation Authority barred a plane carrying Iran's national football team from landing at Basra airport on November 10, 2026. The decision was directly linked to U.S. sanctions imposed on Iranian airlines, according to Basra airport officials.

The Iranian team, en route to a four-nation tournament in Basra, was forced to return to Abadan airport in Iran and will now travel by road. An Iraqi civil aviation official stated that Iraq could not risk violating U.S. sanctions on Iranian airlines, highlighting the increasing impact of these sanctions on Iranian aviation operations in Iraq.

This incident follows a September order by Iraq to suspend Iranian flights to Baghdad airport after the U.S. threatened secondary sanctions against airports and service providers handling Iranian carriers. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had warned that airports servicing Iranian airlines could face sanctions, including exclusion from the U.S. dollar system.

articles.headline: BIS Extends Suspension of 'Affiliates Rule' Until January 10, 2027
body: The U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has further extended the suspension of its 'Affiliates Rule' until January 10, 2027. This rule, originally set to take effect on November 10, 2026, would expand export control restrictions under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to companies owned or controlled by parties on certain restricted party lists.

The 'Affiliates Rule' aims to harmonize BIS ownership and control restrictions with similar rules enforced by OFAC, specifically its '50% Rule,' which prohibits dealings with companies 50% or more owned by sanctioned parties. If implemented, it would significantly increase customer due diligence burdens for companies engaged in transactions involving items subject to the EAR.

The initial suspension of the rule in November 2025 was part of a broader U.S.-China trade agreement. The current extension suggests ongoing negotiations between the two nations, with the ultimate effective date or form of the rule potentially dependent on the outcome of these discussions.

articles.headline: Department of Commerce Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) announced that as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms, easing compliance burdens on the firearms industry while continuing to protect national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also apply to suppressors.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today released enforcement actions for October 2026.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $750 Million Assessment Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.
